aspect: The methodology change, and the two series
description: Under the old methodology unemployment rose from 14.2% in 2016 to 33.3% in 2020. Under the new ILO-aligned methodology, Q2 2024 unemployment was 4.3% with time-related underemployment at 9.2%. The two series are not comparable.
energy_note: Thirty-three per cent, then four, and nothing changed on the ground.

description: Self-employment was 85.6% of employment in Q2 2024 and informal employment was 93.0%. An hour of petty trading in a week counts as employed, which is methodologically correct and tells you nothing about income.
energy_note: Ninety-three per cent informal, and officially employed.

aspect: Women are worse on every sub-measure
description: Q2 2024: unemployment 5.1% female against 3.4% male; youth time-related underemployment 11.2% female against 7.1% male; self-employment 88.3% female against 82.2% male. Higher self-employment here means less formal work, not more entrepreneurship.
energy_note: Worse on unemployment, underemployment and informality, all three.

aspect: The graduate pipeline does not clear
description: Roughly 1.7 million graduates leave Nigerian universities and polytechnics annually without the economy absorbing them.
energy_note: One point seven million graduates a year, into what.

aspect: And the advocacy figures are not reliable either
description: A 2025 youth report claimed nearly 80 million Nigerian youth are unemployed, which is implausible against the NBS rate and appears to conflate unemployment with inactivity and informality. Both the official and the advocacy number mislead in opposite directions.
energy_note: One number too low, one far too high, neither usable.

energy_note: Thirty-three per cent, then four, and the same streets.
